# A Self-Navigating Yacht Aims for Transatlantic History

**LONDON, England (CNN)** -- Engineers have created an "intelligent" sailboat they hope will set a new world record by crossing the Atlantic entirely on its own, with zero human intervention required during the journey.

The vessel, named Avalon, stretches four meters in length and emerged from the efforts of eight engineering students in their third year at ETH Zurich, a leading Swiss technical university. Before her launch, workers can be seen hoisting Avalon into position to install her keel.

The team intends to first showcase the boat at a robotics sailing competition scheduled for July, then attempt the ambitious Microtransat Transatlantic challenge come early September. Avalon relies on onboard sensors that monitor wind speed and direction, allowing her programming to continuously adjust course toward a predetermined destination despite shifting weather conditions.

Hendrik Erckens, who helps manage the "Students Sailing Autonomously" (SSA) initiative, explained to CNN that success in crossing the Atlantic would represent uncharted territory—no unmanned vessel has ever completed such a voyage before. The proposed route would begin along Ireland's western shoreline and conclude somewhere in the Caribbean.

"The Microtransat challenge is really what we're aiming for. I feel quite optimistic about our chances," Erckens noted. "During this week's trials, the boat has performed exactly as intended, and we've confirmed she's fully waterproof. Over recent days, we've experimented with autonomous tacking and jibing maneuvers, and now our focus has shifted to testing the navigation systems."

*Browse images documenting the autonomous yacht's journey from build to launch »*

Work on this venture kicked off back in September 2008, and having completed the design and construction phases, the team now finds itself conducting tests on the water. Although satellite GPS technology will let the team monitor Avalon's position throughout the crossing, Erckens clarified that once the challenge begins, they'll have absolutely no ability to steer or control the boat directly.

"Essentially, we launch her and she operates completely independently from that point forward. Solar panels mounted at the rear provide power, supplemented by backup power reserves stored on board," he explained. "A satellite communication system allows the vessel to pull down weather data on its own, which it then uses to determine the optimal path forward."

According to Erckens, the team feels confident that Avalon's carbon-fiber construction can withstand the notoriously harsh conditions of the Atlantic—conditions that have derailed numerous crewed attempts in the past, including Richard Branson's bid for the fastest transatlantic time aboard his 99-foot vessel Virgin Money last autumn.

"What sets us apart from other competing teams is our background in mechanical engineering. We built this boat ourselves, specifically engineered for this exact mission," he said.

Looking ahead, Erckens suggested this technology might eventually pave the way for advanced autopilot systems suitable for larger sailing vessels. "Autopilot systems already exist commercially for boats, but they're currently limited to controlling just the rudder. Our goal is to extend that control to the sails as well."

This ambitious project showcases the practical application of engineering principles learned throughout their studies, combining expertise in mechanical design, electronics, and software development.

## Technical Design and Capabilities

Measuring four meters in length, Avalon is equipped with sophisticated wind speed and direction sensors that allow the vessel to automatically adjust its sails and course. This technology enables the boat to navigate toward designated coordinates entirely without human intervention or control, representing a genuine feat of autonomous navigation engineering. The sensors continuously feed data to Avalon's onboard systems, which process this information in real-time to make navigational decisions—effectively allowing the boat to "think" and respond to changing wind conditions independently.

## Competition Timeline and Ultimate Goal

The student team has mapped out an ambitious two-phase testing and competition schedule. First, they plan to enter Avalon in a robotic sailing regatta in July, which will serve as a crucial proving ground for the vessel's autonomous systems in a competitive environment. This initial competition will allow the team to identify and address any technical issues before attempting their more audacious goal.

Following the July regatta, the team intends to attempt the prestigious Microtransat Transatlantic Challenge in September. This grueling test will see Avalon attempt to sail unassisted from Ireland to the Caribbean, crossing thousands of kilometers of open ocean entirely on its own. ## Power Systems and Monitoring

To sustain the vessel throughout its extended journey, Avalon is powered by a combination of solar cells and supplementary power supplies, ensuring the boat has sufficient energy for its systems throughout the potentially weeks-long crossing. # Student-Built Autonomous Sailboat Sets Out to Conquer the Atlantic Without Human Hands on Deck

**By CNN Staff**

A team of university engineering students has launched what they're calling their most ambitious project yet: a fully autonomous sailboat designed to cross the Atlantic Ocean without a single person aboard to steer, adjust sails, or intervene if things go wrong.

The vessel, a 20-foot fiberglass hull named *Persistence*, departed from a marina in Plymouth, England, on Tuesday morning, bound for the northeastern coast of the United States. If successful, the roughly 3,000-mile voyage will take an estimated six to eight weeks, depending on wind conditions and the boat's ability to navigate around storms using onboard weather routing software.

"We've basically built a robot that has to make thousands of decisions a day without any way for us to correct it if it makes the wrong one," said Priya Nandakumar, a mechanical engineering senior and the team's project lead. "That's terrifying and exciting in equal measure."

## Years in the Making

The project, dubbed SailBot Atlantic, grew out of a robotics club at the university and has consumed nearly three years of design work, fundraising, and testing. The team — a rotating cast of about 15 students across mechanical engineering, computer science, and environmental science — built the boat almost entirely from scratch, sourcing a bare hull and outfitting it with solar panels, a wind-powered generator, satellite communication equipment, and a suite of sensors that feed into a custom-built navigation computer.

The boat's "brain" runs machine learning models trained on years of historical weather and ocean current data, allowing it to plot and replot its course in real time. A separate collision-avoidance system uses radar and AIS transponder data — the same tracking system used by commercial ships — to detect and steer clear of vessels in its path.

"The hardest part wasn't the sailing, honestly. It was teaching the boat what to do when everything goes wrong at once," said Marcus Webb, a computer science graduate student who led development of the autonomy software. "What happens if the satellite link drops during a storm? What happens if a sensor fails? We had to war-game hundreds of failure scenarios."

## Not the First Attempt

*Persistence* is not the first uncrewed vessel to attempt an Atlantic crossing — Microtransat Challenge competitors have made similar attempts for years, with mixed success, and larger operations like Saildrone have deployed autonomous vessels for ocean research. But the students say their project stands out for being conceived, financed, and built almost entirely by undergraduates, with a budget cobbled together through university grants, a crowdfunding campaign, and donated equipment from marine electronics companies.

Faculty advisor Dr. Elena Voss, a professor of ocean engineering, said the project has doubled as a real-world crash course in systems engineering. "These students have had to become experts in fields they never took a class in — meteorology, maritime law, satellite communications," she said. "The learning that's happened here is honestly more valuable than the crossing itself, whether or not the boat makes it."

## Tracking the Journey

The team is monitoring the boat's progress from a makeshift mission control room on campus, watching data stream in via satellite every few minutes: position, heading, wind speed, battery levels, and internal system diagnostics. A public tracking map has drawn thousands of visitors since launch, with the boat's location visible in near-real time.

Should *Persistence* encounter a critical failure, the team has a contingency plan in place with maritime authorities to attempt recovery, though they acknowledge that in the middle of the ocean, that may not always be feasible.

"We've said from day one that there's a real chance we lose the boat," Nandakumar said. "But even if it doesn't finish, we'll have learned an enormous amount about what it takes to build something that has to survive completely on its own, thousands of miles from anyone who can help it."

If *Persistence* completes the crossing, the team plans to donate the vessel's data to ocean research groups studying autonomous navigation and to open-source portions of their software for future student projects.

For now, the boat sails on alone, its progress marked only by a blinking dot crawling slowly across a map of the open Atlantic.

# ETH Zurich Students Set Sights on Atlantic Crossing with Autonomous Yacht

**LONDON** — A team of engineering students from ETH Zurich is preparing to launch an unmanned sailing vessel across the Atlantic Ocean, joining a growing international field of university researchers competing in the Microtransat Challenge, widely regarded as the "Kon-Tiki" of autonomous maritime robotics.

The Swiss team, working under the university's Autonomous Systems Lab, has spent the past two years designing and testing a small robotic yacht capable of navigating thousands of nautical miles without any human intervention — no crew, no remote piloting, and no possibility of course correction once it departs from shore.

The Microtransat Challenge, first proposed in 2005 by British and French robotics enthusiasts, invites teams to send fully autonomous sailboats across the Atlantic, typically from a launch point in Europe to a finish line in the Caribbean or North America. Despite more than a decade of attempts by teams from Britain, France, Ireland, and the United States, only a handful of vessels have ever successfully completed the crossing, underscoring the immense technical difficulty of the challenge.

"It sounds almost quaint — a small sailboat crossing an ocean — but the engineering problem is brutally hard," said a member of the ETH Zurich team, speaking to reporters ahead of planned sea trials. "You're asking a machine to make thousands of independent decisions about wind, waves, and navigation over several weeks, with no way to intervene if something goes wrong."

The Swiss entry, built largely from carbon-fibre composites to minimise weight while withstanding punishing mid-ocean conditions, relies on a suite of onboard sensors, solar-charged batteries, and custom-written navigation software to hold its course. GPS way-finding is paired with adaptive algorithms that allow the vessel to adjust its sail trim and rudder in response to shifting weather, in theory enabling it to ride out Atlantic storms without human guidance.

Engineering students described the project as an exercise in resilience as much as robotics. Previous Microtransat entries have run aground, capsized, been struck by shipping vessels, or simply vanished — their fate never established. Teams often lose contact with their yachts for days or weeks at a time, relying on intermittent satellite pings to confirm the vessels remain afloat and on course.

"There's a real chance we never see the boat again," one student conceded. "But even a failed attempt generates enormous amounts of data on autonomous navigation, materials performance, and machine decision-making at sea — information that's valuable well beyond sailing."

The ETH Zurich effort reflects a broader trend of European universities using ocean-crossing challenges as proving grounds for autonomous systems technology, with applications that extend into maritime shipping, oceanographic research, and defence. Robotics specialists say the unpredictability of open ocean conditions makes the Microtransat a uniquely demanding test bed — arguably more rigorous than closed-course robotics competitions on land or in controlled waters.

A precise launch date for the Swiss vessel has not yet been finalised, with the team citing the need for further sea trials in more sheltered European waters before committing to a transatlantic attempt. Organisers of the Microtransat Challenge typically designate a launch window in the autumn months, when Atlantic weather patterns are considered comparatively more predictable for small autonomous craft.

If successful, the ETH Zurich yacht would join a short list of vessels — including entries from French and Norwegian teams in recent years — to have completed an unassisted Atlantic crossing, cementing Zurich's engineering programme within a small but growing community pushing the boundaries of maritime autonomy.

# Team of Engineering Students Creates 'Thinking' Yacht That Can Sail Across Oceans Autonomously

*By CNN Staff*

For centuries, sailing across vast stretches of open ocean has demanded human hands on the wheel — constant vigilance, split-second decisions, and an intimate understanding of wind and wave. Now, a team of engineering students says they've built a vessel that can make those decisions on its own.

The team, made up of undergraduate and graduate students from a university engineering program, spent nearly two years designing and testing a self-navigating yacht equipped with GPS tracking, an array of environmental sensors, and onboard computing systems that allow it to adjust course, sail trim, and speed without any human intervention.

"We wanted to build something that could genuinely think for itself out there," said the team's project lead, a senior mechanical engineering student. "Not just follow a pre-programmed route, but actually respond to what the ocean is doing in real time."

## How It Works

The yacht relies on a combination of GPS positioning, wind sensors, accelerometers, and marine radar to build a constantly updating picture of its surroundings. That data feeds into an onboard computer system running custom navigation software, which the students describe as the vessel's "brain."

Unlike traditional autopilot systems, which typically follow fixed waypoints, the students say their system is designed to make more dynamic judgment calls — altering sail configuration in response to shifting winds, rerouting around detected obstacles or storm systems, and optimizing its path for fuel and time efficiency, all without a person on board.

"It's constantly taking in information and recalculating," said one of the team's software engineers. "If the wind shifts 20 degrees, it doesn't just hold its heading blindly. It reassesses and adjusts the sails and rudder to keep making efficient progress."

Solar panels mounted on the deck help power the electronics for extended voyages, reducing the need for the vessel to return to shore for recharging.

## From Classroom Project to Open Water

The idea reportedly began as a classroom capstone project before evolving into a much larger undertaking, with students securing university funding and additional support from engineering faculty mentors.

Early tests were conducted on lakes and coastal waters close to shore, where the team could monitor the yacht from a chase boat and intervene if something went wrong. Over time, testing moved into more open and unpredictable water, with the vessel completing progressively longer unsupervised stretches.

The students say the yacht has since completed test voyages spanning hundreds of nautical miles without direct human control, though they've remained cautious about declaring full ocean crossings until further trials are complete.

"Every test teaches us something new," said the project's lead engineer. "The ocean doesn't care about your algorithm. You have to keep refining it."

## Why It Matters

Autonomous marine vehicles have drawn growing interest in recent years for applications ranging from oceanographic research to search-and-rescue operations and even cargo shipping. Proponents argue that self-navigating vessels could eventually reduce costs, improve safety, and allow researchers to gather data from remote or hazardous waters without risking human crews.

Experts in autonomous systems note that student-led projects like this one, while smaller in scale than commercial efforts by major shipping and defense companies, can serve as valuable proving grounds for new navigation algorithms and sensor integration techniques.

The students say their long-term goal is to demonstrate that a small, low-cost vessel — built largely with off-the-shelf components and open-source software — can achieve a level of autonomous decision-making once reserved for multimillion-dollar research vessels.

"We're not trying to replace human sailors," the project lead said. "We're trying to show what's possible when you give a boat the tools to think through problems on its own."

## What's Next
